sentences.text: That first night they climbed up to the flat roof of the cabin, which his father had reinforced years ago for exactly this purpose.
They took a blanket each and a thermos of hot chocolate, and they lay on their backs side by side.
The sky at 2,600 meters in the middle of the Atacama was not the sky Diego knew from home.
There was no city glow.
There was no moon that night.

There were more stars than he had ever seen, and the Milky Way was a real river across the middle of the sky, thick and pale and dust-colored, with dark places in it that his father said were clouds of gas so far away he could not even do the math on the distance.
"The first rule," his father said, "is that you can only watch it from a place where there is real silence.
No cars.
No people.
It has to be a place where the stars belong.
That is why I bring you here.
My father brought me to a hill in the country when I was your age.
His mother took him to a lake in the south.
It changes with the family.
The land is not the thing.
The silence is the thing."
"The second rule," he went on, "is that when you tell your story, you have to be looking at the constellation.
Not at your notes.
Not at your listener.
At the stars.
You have to look at them the whole time you talk." "The third rule is that the story you add cannot be an important story.
It cannot be about something famous, or something that will change history, or a thing you did that you are proud of.
It has to be something small.
A small true thing.
Because if it is a small true thing, and you tell it looking at the stars, then it becomes big.
That is how it works."
Diego thought about this for a while.
He watched the constellation his father had pointed out earlier — the Cross and its five nearby stars, arranged like a person leaning forward with one hand out.
"What is the first story," he said.
His father was quiet for a moment.
"The first story is my great-grandmother's.
Her name was Rosa.
She said, looking at these stars in 1918: I planted a tree at my house when I was seven years old.
My father did not want me to plant it because it was in a bad place.
I planted it anyway.
He was angry with me for a week.
Then he stopped being angry.
When my father died, he was buried in the shade of that tree.
It was the only shade in the yard by then.
That is what I want to tell."
His father was quiet again, giving Rosa's story time to sit.
Then he said, "The second story is my grandfather's.
His name was Emilio.
He said, looking at these stars in 1946: I had a friend named Tomás when I was nine years old.
We were the same age.
One day we had a fight about a spinning top.
I hit him with a stick and he cried and he ran home.
I never went to his house to say I was sorry.
He moved away with his family six months later.
I have thought about this every year of my life.
That is what I want to tell."
"The third," his father went on, "is my mother's, your grandmother, Ana.
She said, looking at these stars in 1978: I was afraid, for a long time, that I was not a good mother.
My son was quiet and I did not know what he was thinking.
I thought I was doing everything wrong.
One night when he was ten he came into my room while I was reading and he put his hand on my hair, just for a moment, and he went back to bed.
He said nothing.
That was enough to keep me going for a very long time.
That is what I want to tell."
"The fourth," said his father, and his voice went softer, "is mine."
"Mine is: I met your mother in a bookstore in Santiago when we were both twenty.
I was reading a book that I did not really understand, but I wanted to look like the sort of person who would understand it.
She came over and she looked at the book in my hands and she said, this book is very stupid, you should read something better.
I was angry with her for about ten seconds.
Then I laughed.
And I bought a different book.
And I asked her out for coffee.
Everything in my life that has come after that has been because of a small moment when I laughed instead of being embarrassed.
That is what I want to tell."
Diego lay very still.
He had never heard the story of how his parents met before.
He had asked, more than once, and his father had always given a shorter version — we met in a bookstore, we started talking.
Not the whole thing.
Not the part where they laughed.
He turned his head.
He could see his father's face in profile against the stars.
His father was still looking up.
"Papá," said Diego.
"Yes." "Do the stories have to be about family." "No," said his father.
"They just have to be small and true."
For the next twelve days Diego thought about his story.
He walked around the desert during the day with his hands in his pockets, thinking.
He watched his father work — his father spent most of his time in a small office up at the main telescope, checking data and writing reports.
Diego sat in the office some afternoons and read, and thought.
He kept trying to find something that felt right.
But the small true things he could think of all felt very small, and not very true.
Or they felt true but he was not sure why he wanted to tell them.
He asked his father about it, on the eighth day.
"How did you know yours," he said.
His father thought for a moment.
"I did not know it," he said.
"I made it up.
I mean, it was true — it happened.
But I did not know why I wanted to tell that one until I was already telling it.
You have to just start.
You will find out what you meant while you are saying it."
